newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Viag, BT make deal with Telenor.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Viag, BT make deal with Telenor.

text.p: British Telecom Plc and German utility Viag AG said on Thursday that Norway's dominant phone company Telenor Ltd would take a 10 percent stake in their joint telecommunications activities.

The announcement comes two days after Viag and BT were awarded the German government's fourth digital mobile phone licence, which will serve as the cornerstone of their plans to challenge incumbent monopoly Deutsche Telekom AG.

The companies plan to combine wireless and fixed-wire networks to create "metropolitan networks" in eight German regions by the middle of next year as the first step in creating a full-service national telephone network.

The British-German partners will remain the largest investors in the Viag Interkom enterprise and are one of several international alliances gearing up to challenge Telekom when the German telecoms sector is deregulated next year.
"Viag Interkom will be the first major telecommunications company to exploit the convergence between fixed and mobile services," said BT global operations director Alfred Mockett.

Using the latest mobile communications technology, Viag Interkom hopes to build a new kind of phone company that integrates the billing, services and administration of networks that have traditionally been operated separately.
Viag Interkom officials said they will turn their late entry into Germany's booming mobile phone market into an advantage by employing the latest technology.
"The established operators will not be able to create fixed-mobile convergence," said Viag chairman Georg Obermaier.
Mockett saw the advantages but said that in the end the battle would not be won with technology alone.
"Eventually everyone will catch up with each and then it will all be decided over services," he said.

By the middle of next year the company wants to set up networks in Berlin, the greater Hamburg region, Hanover, the Rhine-Ruhr region in the west, the Rhine-Neckar region in the south, Lepzig-Halle in the east, Munich and Nuremberg.

In April, the pieces of the Viag Interkom alliance will be welded into one company. Viag will initially hold 52.5 percent, but wants to give up a stake of around 10 percent to one or more German shareholders who could bring distribution strength to the alliance, lowering its stake to just over 40 percent.
BT would hold 37.5 percent of the group and Telenor would have 10 percent.

Viag Interkom has around 659 customers, including companies such as media group Bertelsmann AG, Compaq Computer, Deutsche Lufthansa, and software group SAP AG, and generated sales of 123 million marks ($75 million) last year, higher than expected.
Obermaier predicted it would achieve up to eight percent market share in the German telecoms sector in 10 years and more than 20 percent of the mobile phone market.
It would invest seven billion marks in the next 10 years and by the year 2007 should generate 10-11 billion marks in sales and break even by 2002.
State-owned Telenor had 1995 revenues of around 4.5 billion marks ($2.7 billion) and with one million subscribers commands 80 percent of the Norwegian mobile phone market.
Like the mouse that roared, the tiny Nordic telecoms group has developed one of the most advanced mobile networks in the world at home and now wants to take that know-how abroad.

"We are working on the assumption that there should be two mobile phones in every home. Today even children have their own mobile phones (in Norway)," said Telenor International chairman Terje Thon. "I cannot see why Germans should not have the same need for telecommunications."
Around 30 percent of the Norway's population of 4.3 million used mobile phones, compared to six percent of Germans. $ = 1.650 German Marks)
